metadata.file_name: 10. Aydoğan & Tat. (2025). Investigating the Performance of Artificial Neural Networks in Predicting Affective Responses .pdf
metadata.venue: Journal of Measurement and Evaluation in Education and Psychology

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for the Lebanese sample (5614 students initially) and then filters the analytic dataset to 4631 students after deleting cases with missing and extreme values to satisfy CFA/ANN assumptions. The manuscript does not report applying PISA complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures; no weight variable name (such as W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) is mentioned. Because the predictive component is implemented via ANN models (neuralnet/nnet/neuralnettools in R, plus Mplus/SPSS), the analysis appears to be conducted without explicit survey-weight incorporation, which is common when ML methods are applied without weight-aware estimation. No additional preprocessing beyond listwise deletion for missing/extreme values and ordinal-to-[0,1] scaling of item responses is described.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because the dependent variables are affective Likert-type item responses from the PISA 2018 intercultural communicative awareness (Awacom) scale (ST218Q01HA–ST218Q07HA), and the study predicts specific item responses (Item3 and Item7) rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores. The paper instead uses CFA to validate the unidimensional latent construct and then trains ANNs to predict responses to other items on the same scale. Missing data handling is addressed via listwise deletion (deleting cases with missing and extreme values) rather than PV-based multiple imputation.
data.outcome_summary: The study trains ANN models on Awacom scale item responses to predict two randomly selected target items: Item3 (ST218Q03HA) and Item7 (ST218Q07HA), using the other six items as inputs. For Item3, the best model (Model1: 70/30 split, one hidden layer with two neurons) yields RMSE values around .618–.623 across all/train/test sets, and sensitivity analysis indicates a relatively linear relationship with other items (except Item7). Similarity between predicted and actual responses is moderate: match ratio ≈ .63 and Kappa ≈ .42 for Item3, with no significant mean difference (marginal homogeneity p > .05). For Item7, the best model (ModelB: 70/30 split, one hidden layer with three neurons) shows higher RMSE (.699–.732) and lower agreement: match ratio ≈ .58 and Kappa ≈ .37 (marginal homogeneity p > .05). In CFA-based validity/reliability checks, predicted-item subsets partially weaken fit indices but remain strong, while explained variance/R-square, factor loadings, and Cronbach’s alpha improve for the latent Awacom construct; predicted values also positively affect reliability.
